text.tspan: Using NeuroRD [5], we built a reaction-diffusion model of calcium (Ca) dynamics (A) in a 21 μm long dendrite (1.2 μm diameter) of a CA1 pyramidal
neuron with a single dendritic spine (with and without the SA) in the middle. Ca2+ regulation included extrusion pumps (PMCA and NCX) and Ca2+
internal buffers (calbindin, calmodulin, fixed buffer). The ER model contained SarcoEndoplasmic Reticulum Ca2+ ATPase type 2 and 3 (SERCA pump),
RyR2s (in the dendrite), RyR3s (in the spine neck), and Ca2+ buffering in the ER. The model also contained mGluR5 activation by glutamate (Glu), IP3
production and IP3R1 activation. The RyR2/RyR3 model accounted for inhibition/activation by calmodulin and was fitted to experimental data [6,7,8].
We simulated synaptic activation as CA2+ and Glu input to the PSD and VGCC activation as Ca2+ input to the dendritic membrane.
Aging in CA1 pyramidal neurons is characterized by increased calcium buffering, RyR2, RyR3, and L-type VGCC expression and increased calmodulin,
resulting in lower RyR3 and PMCA activity and increased RyR2 activity and Ca2+ currents.

The spine apparatus acts as a Ca2+ buffer, stabilizing Ca2+ amplitudes in the spine and dendrite. Activation of RyR3s is crucial for spine-to-dendrite
coupling of Ca2+ transients and allows for activation of calcium induced calcium release in the dendrite.
Opening of RyR3 amplifies Ca transients in the dendrite and increases their spatial spread (blue circles). Ca2+ influx through the VGCCs
further increases the spatial spread of Ca2+ transients (green triangles). For 1 EPSP activation of VGCCs influences Ca2+ spread (green
empty triangles) more than the opening of RyR3 (green filled triangles). Opening of IP3R governs the spatial spread of Ca2+ transients
(purple squares) for stimulation resembling long-term potentiation (LTP) eliciting experimental paradigms.

In old age, 50% of RyR3s are not constitutively bound to calmodulin, which lowers their activation by Ca2, breaking the coupling of Ca2+
signals between the spine and the dendrite. Moreover, high Ca2+ buffering lowers Ca2+ transients in the spine (Fig. above). In old age,
higher activity of L-type VGCCs governs the spread of Ca2+ transients (Fig. below).
